lessons.title: Inputs, events and sequence

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention

We are learning to use inputs, events and sequence to control a micro:bit.

Success criteria

  • I can identify an input and an output.
  • I can explain what starts a button event.
  • I can put instructions in the correct order.

sections.title: Input, event and output
sections.html:
A doorbell helps us understand three computing words.

Input

Information going into a system.

You press the button. The doorbell detects your press.

Event

Something that starts instructions.

The button is pressed. This starts the bell ringing.

Output

Information coming out of a system.

The bell makes a sound. You hear that someone is at the door.

Can the press be both an input and an event?

Yes — it is the same button press.

  • Input tells us what information goes in: the button has been pressed.
  • Event tells us what starts the instructions: the button press happens.

The sound is the output produced in response.

sections.title: Inputs and outputs
sections.html:
A micro:bit can respond to a button press too.

Input: press A

Information goes into the micro:bit.

  • You press button A.
  • The board detects the press.

Output: show a face

Information comes out of the micro:bit.

  • The board lights its LEDs.
  • You see a happy face.

Remember: input goes in; output comes out.

sections.title: An event starts instructions
sections.html:
An event is something happening, such as pressing a button.

In this example, pressing button A starts these three instructions:

On button A pressed

  1. Show a happy face.
  2. Pause for half a second.
  3. Show a heart.

The three instructions sit inside the on button A pressed event block in MakeCode.

  • Before you press A: the face–pause–heart sequence has not started.
  • When you press A: the board runs those three instructions, from 1 to 3.
  • Press A again: the same face–pause–heart sequence starts again.

What about button B?

Button B has its own event block: on button B pressed.

For example, put show a sad face inside that block. Pressing B then shows a sad face; it does not start A’s face–pause–heart sequence.

sections.title: Sequence: the order matters
sections.html:
Sequence means the order in which instructions run.

After you press A, these instructions run from 1 to 3.

1. Show a face

The first image appears.

2. Pause

Keep the face visible for half a second.

3. Show a heart

The heart replaces the face.

  • 500 milliseconds (ms) is half a second.
  • The pause gives you time to see the face.
  • Swap the two image blocks and the heart appears first.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This example shows the order of the blocks. Build it in MakeCode using blocks.

Example structure

on button A pressed:
    show happy face
    pause 500 ms
    show heart

Reading the instructions

on button A pressed

Starts the instructions inside this event when A is pressed.

show happy face

Lights the LEDs to display the first image.

pause 500 ms

Waits half a second before the next instruction in this sequence.

show heart

Replaces the face with a heart; it does not add a second display.

What should happen?

  1. Press A: the happy face appears.
  2. Wait half a second: the face stays on the display.
  3. See the heart: it replaces the face and stays on the display.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
Input
Information goes in: you press button A.
Event
Something happens: the press starts the instructions.
Sequence
Instructions run in order: face, pause, heart.
Output
Information comes out: an image appears on the LEDs.

sections.title: Your workbook tasks
sections.html:
1. Open your workbook

Open the pupil workbook and find Lesson 1.

2. Complete Tasks 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3

  • Create button reactions using images and pauses.
  • Put your blocks in the order you want them to run.
  • Use button events for this lesson.

3. Add your evidence

  • Show your button event and its blocks.
  • Label one input and one output.
  • Explain why the order matters.

Need help with the blocks?

lessons.title: Variables and random numbers

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention: Store a number in a variable and explain how a random range works.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Explain the difference between setting and reading a variable.
  • Identify every possible value in a random range.
  • Trace the saved value through a shake and two button presses.

Read one page at a time. Predict before checking the explanations. Your practical tasks are in your workbook.

sections.title: The idea in everyday life
sections.html: Imagine a scoreboard with the label score above a number. The label stays the same while the number changes. A variable works in a similar way: it gives a stored value a name so the program can use it later.

sections.title: A name for a stored value
sections.html:
Create a variable called roll. Setting roll to 4 stores 4 under that name. Setting it to 2 later replaces 4; it does not keep both numbers. A show number roll block reads the value currently stored in roll. Displaying a value does not change it.

Key word: Variable

A name used to store a value.

sections.title: Choose once, use again
sections.html:
Pick random 1 to 6 chooses a whole number from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. Both limits are included. Put that block inside set roll so the chosen result is saved. If you put a fresh random block inside every display block, each display can choose a different number.

Key word: Random range

The allowed values from which a random result is chosen.

sections.title: Give the program a starting value
sections.html:
Put set roll to 1 in on start. This gives the dice a clear starting value before anyone shakes the board. The shake event replaces it with a random roll. Button A reads the saved roll. Random results can repeat: getting 4 twice does not show that the program is broken.

Key word: Initialise

Give a variable its starting value.

sections.title: Follow it on the micro:bit
sections.html: Shaking chooses and stores a new roll. Pressing A displays the stored value without rolling again. Set roll to 1 at startup so A also has a value before the first shake.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This is pseudocode describing the MakeCode Blocks. Rebuild it using blocks; it is not code to paste into the editor. Any setup or surrounding events described on the previous pages are also needed.

Example structure

on start:
    set roll to 1
on shake:
    set roll to pick random 1 to 6
    show number roll
on button A pressed:
    show number roll

Reading the instructions

on start → set roll to 1

Gives the saved result a known starting value.

on shake

Starts a new roll when the board detects a shake.

set roll to pick random 1 to 6

Chooses one allowed number and replaces the saved value.

show number roll

Displays the saved value. In the A event this reads it without rolling again.

What should happen?

After startup, A displays 1. Suppose a shake chooses 4: the board shows 4 and roll stores 4. Two A presses both show 4. A later shake may choose a different number, or choose 4 again.

Watch out

Do not use change roll by with a random number for a dice. That adds to the old result and can produce values above 6. Use set roll to replace it.

sections.title: Predict, trace and check
sections.html:
If roll stores 4, what will two A presses display? Can 0 or 7 be generated by the stated range?

Explain your prediction before trying the program. Follow the event one instruction at a time, keeping track of any stored values.

Check your reasoning

Both A presses display 4. Neither 0 nor 7 is inside the inclusive range 1 to 6. Thirty valid rolls check the range but do not prove that every result is equally likely.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
Choose a value, store it, then read that same value when you need it.

Can you explain it?

  • I can explain the difference between setting and reading a variable.
  • I can identify every possible value in a random range.
  • I can trace the saved value through a shake and two button presses.

Return to the example if you cannot yet explain one of these points. Use the key words to explain what the blocks do, rather than only describing where to click.

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Build the dice without an if block. Record 30 rolls and check every result is between 1 and 6. Keep this project for Lesson 3.

Evidence and explanation: Explain what roll stores and the difference between generating a new value and displaying the stored value.

Complete Tasks 2.1, 2.2 and 2.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

Practical references

These guides retain their original project numbers; those numbers are not the new teaching lesson numbers. Use the relevant tasks described below.

  • Dice reference: use the corrected dice in Task 2; investigate its faulty condition in Lesson 3.

Back to the teaching sequence

lessons.title: Selection and comparisons

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention: Use an if condition to choose whether instructions run.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Write a comparison and explain when it is true.
  • Trace both branches of an if / else decision.
  • Explain why replacing every 6 with 1 makes the dice unfair.

Read one page at a time. Predict before checking the explanations. Your practical tasks are in your workbook.

sections.title: The idea in everyday life
sections.html: A sign might say: if the pool is open, go swimming; otherwise, choose another activity. Only one of those paths is followed. A program uses a condition to choose a path too.

sections.title: A question with two answers
sections.html:
A condition is a check whose result is true or false. The comparison roll = 6 asks whether the saved roll equals 6. It does not put 6 into roll. In MakeCode Blocks, the comparison block and set variable block have different shapes and jobs.

Key word: Condition

A check with a true or false result.

sections.title: Choose one branch
sections.html:
An if / else block has two branches. When its condition is true, the instructions inside if run. When false, the instructions inside else run instead. After the selected branch finishes, the program continues after the whole decision. Both branches do not run for the same check.

Key word: Selection

Choosing instructions by checking a condition.

sections.title: Read the stored result
sections.html:
Keep the dice from Lesson 2. Button B checks the result already stored in roll. A result of 6 shows a happy face; any other result is displayed as a number. Greater than and less than compare size: roll > 3 is true for 4, 5 and 6, but false for 3.

Key word: Comparison

A check such as equal to, greater than or less than.

sections.title: Follow it on the micro:bit
sections.html: Continue with the dice from Lesson 2. Button B checks the stored roll; it does not generate another number. The else branch runs when roll is not 6.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This is pseudocode describing the MakeCode Blocks. Rebuild it using blocks; it is not code to paste into the editor. Any setup or surrounding events described on the previous pages are also needed.

Example structure

on button B pressed:
    if roll = 6:
        show happy face
    else:
        show number roll

Reading the instructions

on button B pressed

Starts the check; it does not roll the dice again.

if roll = 6

Reads roll and compares it with 6.

show happy face

Runs only when the condition is true.

else → show number roll

Runs when the saved value is not 6.

What should happen?

With roll set to 6, B shows a face and roll still stores 6. With roll set to 2, B shows 2. To check both branches reliably, temporarily set known values rather than waiting for random rolls.

Watch out

Changing every generated 6 to 1 makes 6 impossible to display and gives 1 an extra way to occur. The fault is in the rule after the random choice, even if the random block itself is correct.

sections.title: Predict, trace and check
sections.html:
Trace the event for roll = 6 and roll = 2. Does displaying a face change the value stored in roll?

Explain your prediction before trying the program. Follow the event one instruction at a time, keeping track of any stored values.

Check your reasoning

For 6 the condition is true, so the face appears. For 2 it is false, so 2 appears. Neither display instruction changes roll.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
A condition checks a value. Selection chooses the instructions to run.

Can you explain it?

  • I can write a comparison and explain when it is true.
  • I can trace both branches of an if / else decision.
  • I can explain why replacing every 6 with 1 makes the dice unfair.

Return to the example if you cannot yet explain one of these points. Use the key words to explain what the blocks do, rather than only describing where to click.

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Add a decision to your existing dice. Then inspect the faulty rule that changes every 6 to 1 and explain why it makes the dice unfair.

Evidence and explanation: Include your condition, predictions for both outcomes and actual test results.

Complete Tasks 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

lessons.title: Iteration

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention: Explain counted repetition and distinguish it from continuous repetition.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Count how often an instruction inside a loop runs.
  • Identify which instructions belong to the loop body.
  • Choose between counted and continuous repetition.

Read one page at a time. Predict before checking the explanations. Your practical tasks are in your workbook.

sections.title: The idea in everyday life
sections.html: A dance routine might say clap, stamp, repeat three times. You do not need to write the same pair of actions three times. A loop lets a program repeat a group of instructions.

sections.title: Repeat a known number of times
sections.html:
Iteration means repeating instructions. A repeat 3 times block runs all the instructions inside it, returns to the top, and does that until three complete passes have finished. Instructions after the loop run once the counted repetition ends.

Key word: Iteration

Repeating instructions.

sections.title: Check what is inside
sections.html:
The loop body contains both images and both pauses. One pass shows a large diamond, waits, shows a small diamond, then waits again. Three passes run six show instructions and six pause instructions. Moving a block outside the loop changes how often it runs.

Key word: Loop body

The group of instructions inside a loop.

sections.title: Keep checking with forever
sections.html:
A forever block repeats while the program runs. It suits a sensor display because the light level can change at any time. Read light level inside the loop to get a fresh reading each pass. A pause spaces the updates so the display is usable. Use a separate project for this example so two loops do not compete for the display.

Key word: Forever

A loop that continues while the program runs.

sections.title: Follow it on the micro:bit
sections.html: Return to the character from Lesson 1 and add the shake animation. Both show blocks and both pauses belong inside the loop. Later, try a separate forever example that repeatedly displays the light level.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This is pseudocode describing the MakeCode Blocks. Rebuild it using blocks; it is not code to paste into the editor. Any setup or surrounding events described on the previous pages are also needed.

Example structure

on shake:
    repeat 3 times:
        show diamond
        pause 200 ms
        show small diamond
        pause 200 ms

Reading the instructions

on shake

Starts one counted animation.

repeat 3 times

Repeats the whole enclosed sequence three times.

show diamond → pause 200 ms

Shows the large frame for one fifth of a second.

show small diamond → pause 200 ms

Shows the small frame before the next pass starts.

What should happen?

One shake produces three large-to-small animation cycles. The pauses total 1,200 ms across the three cycles, plus any time used by other blocks. After the last pause, the small diamond remains.

Watch out

A forever loop does not stop after three passes. Choose repeat when an animation must finish, and forever when a program must keep checking or updating.

sections.title: Predict, trace and check
sections.html:
How many image instructions run after one shake? How is repeat 3 different from forever?

Explain your prediction before trying the program. Follow the event one instruction at a time, keeping track of any stored values.

Check your reasoning

Six image instructions run: two in each of three passes. Repeat 3 finishes; forever keeps repeating until the program stops or restarts.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
The loop repeats everything inside it, in order.

Can you explain it?

  • I can count how often an instruction inside a loop runs.
  • I can identify which instructions belong to the loop body.
  • I can choose between counted and continuous repetition.

Return to the example if you cannot yet explain one of these points. Use the key words to explain what the blocks do, rather than only describing where to click.

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Add and test the counted animation. In a separate example, use forever to show the light level, pause 500 ms, then repeat automatically as you cover and uncover the display.

Evidence and explanation: Show both loop structures and explain when each is useful.

Complete Tasks 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

lessons.title: Boolean logic and state

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention: Use true/false values to record state and combine checks with AND.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Explain what armed and triggered each remember.
  • Predict all four combinations of two AND checks.
  • Use measured light readings to choose and test a threshold.

Read one page at a time. Predict before checking the explanations. Your practical tasks are in your workbook.

sections.title: The idea in everyday life
sections.html: Think of an alarm that can be switched on or off. Opening a box should trigger it only while it is armed. The program must remember both whether it is armed and whether it has already detected a problem.

sections.title: Remember a true or false state
sections.html:
A Boolean value is either true or false. Use armed to remember whether monitoring is enabled, and triggered to remember whether the alarm has detected light. These variables describe different things. On start, set both to false. Button A clears triggered before setting armed to true; button B sets both false and clears the display.

Key word: Boolean

A value that is either true or false.

sections.title: Combine checks with AND
sections.html:
The condition armed AND light level > threshold needs both parts to be true. Bright light while disarmed must not trigger the alarm. An armed board in darkness must not trigger it either. First measure covered and uncovered readings, then choose a threshold between them. The right threshold depends on your classroom and covering.

Key word: AND

True only when both combined checks are true.

sections.title: Remember an earlier event
sections.html:
When the trigger condition is true, set triggered to true. The next check flashes the display while armed AND triggered. Covering the board again makes the light check false but does not set triggered back to false. This remembered state lets the alarm report an opening even after the box closes. NOT reverses a Boolean result: NOT false is true.

Key word: State

Stored information about the current situation of a program.

sections.title: Follow it on the micro:bit
sections.html: Set armed and triggered to false at startup. Button A clears triggered then sets armed to true. Button B sets both to false and clears the display. Once triggered is true, covering the display does not reset it.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This is pseudocode describing the MakeCode Blocks. Rebuild it using blocks; it is not code to paste into the editor. Any setup or surrounding events described on the previous pages are also needed.

Example structure

forever:
    if armed AND light level > threshold:
        set triggered to true
    if armed AND triggered:
        show cross
        pause 200 ms
        clear screen
        pause 200 ms

Reading the instructions

if armed AND light level > threshold

Checks that monitoring is enabled and the reading is above the chosen limit.

set triggered to true

Remembers the detection, even if the light level later falls.

if armed AND triggered

Allows flashing only when both states are true.

show cross / clear screen, with pauses

Alternates the warning and a blank display so the warning flashes.

What should happen?

With armed false, bright light produces no trigger. Arm the board in darkness, then expose it to light: triggered becomes true and flashing begins. Cover it again: flashing continues. B disarms and clears the alarm.

Watch out

Do not add an else that sets triggered to false whenever the reading drops. That would forget the opening as soon as the box closes. Reset it deliberately in the button handlers.

sections.title: Predict, trace and check
sections.html:
Will the alarm trigger when armed is false? Why does it keep flashing after the light drops?

Explain your prediction before trying the program. Follow the event one instruction at a time, keeping track of any stored values.

Check your reasoning

A disarmed alarm cannot pass the AND check. Flashing continues after the light drops because triggered remembers the earlier detection until reset.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
A sensor tells you what is happening now. State can remember what happened earlier.

Can you explain it?

  • I can explain what armed and triggered each remember.
  • I can predict all four combinations of two AND checks.
  • I can use measured light readings to choose and test a threshold.

Return to the example if you cannot yet explain one of these points. Use the key words to explain what the blocks do, rather than only describing where to click.

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Measure covered and uncovered light readings. Choose a threshold between them, then build and test the armed alarm.

Evidence and explanation: Record your threshold, a test while disarmed, a trigger test and a stop test. Explain what each Boolean variable records.

lessons.title: Coordinates and boundaries

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention: Use display coordinates and conditions to keep a moving dot within the screen.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Locate an LED using x and y coordinates.
  • Explain why valid coordinates run from 0 to 4.
  • Trace a boundary check before changing the position.

Read one page at a time. Predict before checking the explanations. Your practical tasks are in your workbook.

sections.title: The idea in everyday life
sections.html: A seat in a cinema is found using two pieces of information: its position across and its row. An LED on the micro:bit also needs two coordinates so the program knows exactly which light to use.

sections.title: Find a point on the grid
sections.html:
The display has five columns and five rows. Both are numbered 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The x coordinate counts across from the left; y counts down from the top. The top-left LED is (0, 0) and the bottom-right is (4, 4). In this project y stays at 4, so the player moves along the bottom row.

Key word: Coordinate

A number specifying a position along an axis.

sections.title: Change a stored position
sections.html:
Start x at 2 so the dot begins in the middle. A sufficiently strong left tilt changes x by -1; a right tilt changes it by 1. The acceleration x reading measures tilt along that axis. The stored variable x is the chosen display column: it has a different job from the sensor reading.

Key word: Axis

A direction used to measure position: x across, y down.

sections.title: Check before moving
sections.html:
Before moving left, check x > 0. Before moving right, check x < 4. Each movement also needs the appropriate tilt check, joined with AND. Clear the previous display, plot the new position, then pause 200 ms. Without clearing, old dots remain; without a pause, movement can reach an edge too quickly to control.

Key word: Boundary

The limit of the valid positions.

sections.title: Follow it on the micro:bit
sections.html: The player stays on row 4 while x changes. Start with this moving dot; scoring and reset routines can be added later.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This is pseudocode describing the MakeCode Blocks. Rebuild it using blocks; it is not code to paste into the editor. Any setup or surrounding events described on the previous pages are also needed.

Example structure

on start:
    set x to 2
forever:
    if acceleration x < -300 AND x > 0:
        change x by -1
    if acceleration x > 300 AND x < 4:
        change x by 1
    clear screen
    plot x, 4
    pause 200 ms

Reading the instructions

set x to 2

Starts in the middle column.

acceleration x < -300 AND x > 0

Requires both a left tilt and space to move left.

acceleration x > 300 AND x < 4

Requires both a right tilt and space to move right.

clear screen → plot x, 4 → pause 200 ms

Redraws one dot on the bottom row and spaces the movement checks.

What should happen?

At startup the dot appears at (2, 4). Holding a left tilt moves it through columns 1 and 0. Continued left tilt leaves it at 0. A right tilt can move it back across to 4, where the other boundary check stops it.

Watch out

There are five columns, but column 5 does not exist. Numbering starts at 0. Checking x < 5 would allow a move from 4 to 5, taking the saved position outside the visible grid.

sections.title: Predict, trace and check
sections.html:
At x = 0, what happens on a left tilt? Where is the point 2, 4?

Explain your prediction before trying the program. Follow the event one instruction at a time, keeping track of any stored values.

Check your reasoning

At x = 0, the left boundary condition is false, so x stays 0. The point (2, 4) is the middle LED on the bottom row.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
Check the boundary before changing the position.

Can you explain it?

  • I can locate an LED using x and y coordinates.
  • I can explain why valid coordinates run from 0 to 4.
  • I can trace a boundary check before changing the position.

Return to the example if you cannot yet explain one of these points. Use the key words to explain what the blocks do, rather than only describing where to click.

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Build the moving dot and test both edges repeatedly. Reuse your conditions, loop and variable knowledge.

Evidence and explanation: Label the axes, explain one boundary condition and record the results at both edges.

lessons.title: Functions

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention: Define a named group of instructions, call it and explain why reuse is useful.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Distinguish a function definition from a call.
  • Trace what changes when resetGame runs.
  • Explain how reuse makes an update easier.

Read one page at a time. Predict before checking the explanations. Your practical tasks are in your workbook.

sections.title: The idea in everyday life
sections.html: A recipe gives a useful set of instructions a name. You can follow the recipe again without writing it out every time. A function gives a reusable group of program instructions a name.

sections.title: Define a useful group
sections.html:
Create a function named resetGame. Put the instructions for returning the game to its starting state inside it: set x to 2, set score to 0, and clear the screen. Defining the function describes what it does. It does not run the reset just because the definition exists.

Key word: Function

A named group of instructions.

sections.title: Call it when needed
sections.html:
A call tells the program to run the function now. Call resetGame from on start, and call it again from on button A pressed. Each call runs the same instructions. When they finish, execution continues after the call. In the tilt game, the forever loop will plot the player using the reset position.

Key word: Call

An instruction to run a function.

sections.title: Change the behaviour in one place
sections.html:
If the game later has a target or a game-over state, include their reset instructions in resetGame too. Both startup and the A button will then use the updated reset. A descriptive name helps you read the program: resetGame tells you more than function1. This example uses a function for its actions; it does not need to return a value.

Key word: Reuse

Use the same instructions from more than one place.

sections.title: Follow it on the micro:bit
sections.html: Continue the tilt project. Put the reset instructions in one function and call it at startup and from button A. If both places need the same reset behaviour, you only need to edit the function once.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This is pseudocode describing the MakeCode Blocks. Rebuild it using blocks; it is not code to paste into the editor. Any setup or surrounding events described on the previous pages are also needed.

Example structure

function resetGame:
    set x to 2
    set score to 0
    clear screen
on start:
    call resetGame
on button A pressed:
    call resetGame

Reading the instructions

function resetGame

Defines the named instructions.

set x to 2 / set score to 0

Restores the starting position and score.

on start → call resetGame

Resets the game when the program starts.

on button A pressed → call resetGame

Uses the same reset whenever A is pressed.

What should happen?

Startup sets x to 2 and score to 0. Suppose the player later reaches x = 4 with score = 7. Pressing A restores x = 2 and score = 0. The definition is shared; it is not copied into each event.

Watch out

A definition with no calls never performs the reset. Also check that all reset instructions are inside the function, rather than leaving one only in on start.

sections.title: Predict, trace and check
sections.html:
Does defining resetGame run it? Where is it called? What changes at both call sites if you add an instruction inside it?

Explain your prediction before trying the program. Follow the event one instruction at a time, keeping track of any stored values.

Check your reasoning

Defining resetGame does not run it. Startup and A each call it. An extra instruction inside the function runs at both call sites the next time each calls it.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
Define the instructions once. Call them wherever they are needed.

Can you explain it?

  • I can distinguish a function definition from a call.
  • I can trace what changes when resetGame runs.
  • I can explain how reuse makes an update easier.

Return to the example if you cannot yet explain one of these points. Use the key words to explain what the blocks do, rather than only describing where to click.

sections.title: Apply it in your workbook
sections.html:
Create resetGame, move your reset instructions inside it and call it from startup and button A. Use a name that describes its purpose.

Evidence and explanation: Show the function and its two calls. Explain the difference between defining and calling it.

  • Later reuse: showReady is another named group of instructions.

sections.html: Imagine a playlist. It stores several items in an order, and the same song could appear more than once. A list lets a program store an ordered collection rather than giving every item a separate variable.

sections.title: Values and positions are different
sections.html:

set position to 0

lessons.title: Radio communication

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention: Send and receive agreed messages between two micro:bits.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Trace a request and acknowledgement across two programs.
  • Explain why groups and message text must agree.
  • Explain what the request counter does and does not measure.

Read one page at a time. Predict before checking the explanations. Your practical tasks are in your workbook.

sections.title: The idea in everyday life
sections.html: Two people using walkie-talkies need the same channel and an agreement about their messages. Hearing a message is only useful if the receiver knows what it means. The two micro:bit programs need that agreement too.

sections.title: Agree a group and message
sections.html:
Both boards must set the same teacher-allocated radio group in on start. Agree that HELP requests assistance and OK acknowledges it. These strings must match exactly, including capitals. A radio group helps organise classroom messages; it does not identify an individual pupil or provide a private connection.

Key word: Radio group

A setting used to group radio communication.

sections.title: Sending and receiving are separate
sections.html:
On the pupil board, A sends HELP. On the teacher board, on radio received runs when a message arrives. The receivedString value holds that message. Check it before responding, so an unrelated string does not count as a request. Keep the two programs clearly named so you download each to the intended board.

Key word: Message

Information sent from one board to another.

sections.title: Follow the reply and the count
sections.html:
Initialise requests to 0 on the teacher board. Each received HELP adds 1. Teacher B sends OK, and the pupil shows a tick when OK is received. The count records messages, not unique pupils: one pupil sending HELP three times adds three. If several pupils share a group, the simple OK reply does not identify which pupil it is for.

Key word: Receive event

Instructions started by an arriving radio message.

sections.title: Follow it on the micro:bit
sections.html: Pupil A sends HELP. Teacher B sends OK. The pupil displays a tick when OK arrives. Text must match exactly, including capitals. The counter records requests, not different pupils.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This is pseudocode describing the MakeCode Blocks. Rebuild it using blocks; it is not code to paste into the editor. Any setup or surrounding events described on the previous pages are also needed.

Example structure

on radio received receivedString:
    if receivedString = "HELP":
        change requests by 1
        show string "H"

Reading the instructions

on start → radio set group

Must use the allocated matching group on both boards.

pupil A → radio send string "HELP"

Sends a request; it does not directly change the other board’s variables.

if receivedString = "HELP"

Checks the content of the arriving message.

change requests by 1 → show string "H"

Counts the request and indicates that help was requested.

What should happen?

After one received HELP, the teacher count is 1 and H appears. Teacher B sends OK; the pupil receives it and shows a tick. Another HELP increases the count again, even if it came from the same pupil.

Watch out

A successful send block does not prove a reply arrived. If the receiver does nothing, check power, the downloaded program, matching groups and exact message text, then test the journey again on two boards.

sections.title: Predict, trace and check
sections.html:
Which event sends HELP? Which event handles it? Why can two boards with different groups fail to communicate?

Explain your prediction before trying the program. Follow the event one instruction at a time, keeping track of any stored values.

Check your reasoning

Pupil A sends HELP. The teacher’s receive event handles it. Different groups prevent this intended exchange. Repeated requests increase a message count rather than a count of distinct pupils.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
Agree the message, send it, then handle it in the receiver’s event.

Can you explain it?

  • I can trace a request and acknowledgement across two programs.
  • I can explain why groups and message text must agree.
  • I can explain what the request counter does and does not measure.

Return to the example if you cannot yet explain one of these points. Use the key words to explain what the blocks do, rather than only describing where to click.

sections.html:
Build the pupil and teacher help programs. Test the request, acknowledgement and repeated requests. Save them for Lesson 10.

Evidence and explanation: Draw the message journey, include both programs and record what happens after repeated A presses.

Complete Tasks 9.1, 9.2 and 9.3 in the Google Docs pupil workbook. Use the lesson heading to find your tasks.

lessons.title: Integration, testing and evaluation

sections.title: Learning intention & success criteria
sections.html:
Learning intention: Combine earlier concepts, prevent duplicate requests and evaluate against requirements.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Write a test with an expected and an actual result.
  • Trace waiting through a request and its acknowledgement.
  • Use test evidence to evaluate a requirement and explain a limitation.

Read one page at a time. Predict before checking the explanations. Your practical tasks are in your workbook.

sections.title: The idea in everyday life
sections.html: Testing a new door lock once is not enough. You would check that the right key opens it, the wrong key does not, and locking it again still works. A program also needs tests for different situations, including actions it should reject.

sections.title: Turn a requirement into a test
sections.html:
A requirement states what the system must do. For example: while waiting for a reply, repeated A presses must not send extra requests. A useful test records the starting state, the action, the expected result and the actual result. Write the expected result before running the test so you have something clear to compare.

Key word: Requirement

A statement of what the system must do.

sections.title: Use state to prevent duplicates
sections.html:
Set waiting to false at startup. In the A event, check NOT waiting. On the first press this is true: set waiting to true before sending HELP. Further presses see waiting true, so NOT waiting is false and no extra request is sent. Receiving OK sets waiting false and allows a new request.

Key word: Debugging

Finding and repairing faults in a program.

sections.title: Repair, retest and evaluate
sections.html:
Keep the teacher counter so you can observe duplicate requests. If a result differs from the prediction, trace the event and stored values, change the faulty instructions, then repeat that test and related tests. Evaluation explains how well the requirements were met using results. Name a limitation too: without a received reply, this simple pupil program stays waiting; it has no automatic timeout.

Key word: Evaluation

Judging how well requirements were met, using evidence.

sections.title: Follow it on the micro:bit
sections.html: Set waiting to false at startup. Setting it true before sending closes the opportunity for another request while waiting. Keep the teacher counter so you can prove that repeated presses do not send duplicates.

sections.title: Example explained
sections.html:
This is pseudocode describing the MakeCode Blocks. Rebuild it using blocks; it is not code to paste into the editor. Any setup or surrounding events described on the previous pages are also needed.

Example structure

on button A pressed:
    if NOT waiting:
        set waiting to true
        radio send string "HELP"
        show question mark
on radio received receivedString:
    if receivedString = "OK":
        set waiting to false
        show tick

Reading the instructions

if NOT waiting

Allows a request only when the pupil is ready.

set waiting to true → send "HELP"

Records the pending request before another press can send one.

if receivedString = "OK"

Checks that the incoming message is the acknowledgement.

set waiting to false → show tick

Allows another request and displays confirmation.

What should happen?

Start both programs with the teacher count at 0. One A press followed by three more before any reply should leave the count at 1. After teacher B sends OK and the pupil receives it, a new A press should increase the count to 2.

Watch out

Showing a question mark does not remember that a request is pending. The condition must check waiting, and OK must reset waiting. Otherwise duplicates may be allowed, or the pupil may never be able to request help again.

sections.title: Predict, trace and check
sections.html:
After one request and three more A presses, what should the teacher count show? What must happen before another request is allowed?

Explain your prediction before trying the program. Follow the event one instruction at a time, keeping track of any stored values.

Check your reasoning

The teacher count should be 1, assuming that the first HELP arrived once and no other sender contributed. The pupil must receive OK before it can send another request.

sections.title: What to remember
sections.html:
Predict, test, compare, repair and retest. Use the evidence in your evaluation.

Can you explain it?

  • I can write a test with an expected and an actual result.
  • I can trace waiting through a request and its acknowledgement.
  • I can use test evidence to evaluate a requirement and explain a limitation.

sections.title: Learning intention
sections.html:
Learning intention: Program a character that reacts to buttons using inputs, events and sequence.

Key ideas: Events; sequence; inputs; processing; outputs

Time: 55 minutes.

sections.title: Related teaching pages
sections.html:
This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 1: Inputs, events and sequence

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:
• Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

sections.title: Task 1: Start your project
sections.html:
1. Open MakeCode for micro:bit and choose New Project. Name it S1-01-Personality. Stay in Blocks.
  2. Keep on start. Remove the empty forever block by dragging it back into the toolbox.
  3. From Basic, put show icon inside on start. Choose a heart. The start event runs when the program starts or the board resets.

sections.title: Task 2: Create two button sequences
sections.html:
1. From Input, add on button A pressed. Inside it, show a happy face, pause 500 ms, then show a heart.
  2. Add another button event and select B. Inside it, show a sad face, pause 500 ms, then show a diamond.
  3. Predict the image order for each button, then test in the simulator.
  4. Swap the two images in one event. Predict and test the difference, then restore your chosen order.

sections.title: Task 3: Use the real micro:bit
sections.html:
1. Connect the board with a USB data cable. Follow the download instructions in the Getting Started guide.
  2. Try each button separately. Wait for its sequence to finish before trying the other button.
  3. Change the startup icon and the two button reactions to suit your character. Keep both button events.
  4. Save your project and download a backup .hex file. Complete workbook lesson 1.

sections.title: Test your program
sections.html:
Test Expected result

sections.title: Before you start
sections.html:

  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".

sections.title: Task 1: Agree the message meaning
sections.html:
1. Use two boards and one allocated radio group. Create S1-08-Sender and S1-08-Receiver.
  2. Agree this codebook: 1 = need help; 2 = task finished; 3 = please check. Writing a meaning as a number is encoding, not encryption.
  3. In both programs, make a variable key and set it to 7 in on start. Also set the same radio group in both.

sections.title: Task 2: Build SENDER
sections.html:
1. Create a variable message and set it to 1 in on start.
  2. On button A pressed: change message by 1; if message > 3 then set message to 1; show number message.
  3. On button B pressed: radio send number message + key, then show icon Yes.
  4. Use A to choose a message and B to send it.

sections.title: Task 3: Build RECEIVER
sections.html:
1. Create a variable decoded. Add on radio received receivedNumber. This is the NUMBER event, not the string event.
  2. Inside: set decoded to receivedNumber - key. Then show number decoded. Use the codebook to interpret it.
  3. Send all three messages. Record the original value, transmitted value and decoded value in the workbook.
  4. Temporarily change RECEIVER key to 6. Send message 2. Record the incorrect result, then restore key 7.
  5. Another pair is told that the transmitted value was 9 and the original was 2. Ask them to find the key. Save and screenshot both programs.

sections.title: Task 4: Explain the security
sections.html:
1. The add/subtract rule is a toy encryption model for learning. It is very easy to break and must not protect real secrets.
  2. A group number does not hide message contents. An observer using the same group can receive the transmitted number.
  3. Discuss how knowing one original/transmitted pair reveals this key.

sections.html:
Test Expected result
Send 1 with key 7 Transmitted 8; receiver displays 1.
Send 2 with key 7 Transmitted 9; receiver displays 2.
Send 3 with key 7 Transmitted 10; receiver displays 3.
Sender key 7; receiver key 6; send 2 Receiver displays 3, showing the wrong meaning.
Restore both keys to 7 Original meaning is recovered.

sections.title: Complete your workbook
sections.html:
• Screenshot: Complete SENDER program.
  • Screenshot: Complete RECEIVER program.

Answer these questions in your own words:

  1. What is the difference between the codebook and the shared key?
  2. How can someone find the key if 2 is transmitted as 9?
  3. Could the number 1 have another meaning in a different system?

Learning intention: Prevent duplicate requests, reuse a function and evaluate against requirements.

Key ideas: Boolean state; selection; subprograms; systematic testing

Time: 55 minutes.

Related teaching pages

This is a practical reference with its original project number. Your teacher will choose the relevant tasks for the new teaching sequence.

  • Lesson 7: Functions
  • Lesson 10: Integration, testing and evaluation

Before you start

  • Work in MakeCode Blocks.
  • Use the exact project and variable names below. = in a condition means "is equal to".
  • set replaces a stored value; change by adds to the current value.
  • Put a block inside a condition or loop when the instruction says so. Indentation matters.
  • If the task uses radio, both boards need power and the same allocated group. No internet or Bluetooth pairing is needed between the boards.
  • Keep the board close to the desk. Do not throw it, pull its USB cable or cover it with metal.

Task 1: Make a separate improved version

  1. Open each lesson 9 project and save a copy named S1-10-Pupil or S1-10-Teacher. If your editor does not offer duplicate, download a .hex backup then rename the open project.
  2. Keep the teacher counter from lesson 9. It is how you will prove duplicate requests are blocked.
  3. In the PUPIL program, create a variable waiting. In on start, set waiting to false after the radio group is set.

Task 2: Guard the request

  1. In PUPIL on button A pressed, wrap the existing send and icon blocks inside if NOT waiting. Find not in Logic.
  2. At the TOP of that if branch, set waiting to true. Then send HELP and show Question. Changing the state first closes the duplicate-request window.
  3. In the received OK branch, add set waiting to false before showing the tick.

Task 3: Reuse the ready display

  1. Make a function showReady with no extra input spaces. Inside: clear screen, then show icon SmallSquare.
  2. Call showReady at the end of on start.
  3. Add pupil on button B pressed. Inside, if NOT waiting, call showReady. B returns the idle display to ready after acknowledgement; it cannot cancel an outstanding request.
  4. The teacher program stays as lesson 9. Rename it clearly and download both programs.

Task 4: Test and evaluate

  1. Reset BOTH boards and wait for startup. Use the complete test table below in order.
  2. Record actual results; do not write Pass until you have performed each test.
  3. If a test fails, record the fault, change the code and repeat that test.
  4. Take final screenshots of BOTH programs, including the function. Answer the workbook questions individually even if you shared boards.
  5. Finish with two sentences: which requirements were met, and one limitation of this prototype.
